lesson.title: Containers from Zero, part 1: what a container is
lesson.description: A container is an ordinary Linux process with its own view of files, processes, network and hostname. Install Docker Engine and Compose, then find one container from inside and from the host.
lesson.tested: Installed Docker Engine 29.10.1 and Compose v5.8.0 on Ubuntu 24.04 and ran every lab command, 25 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: A container is a process the kernel shows a smaller world. Keep that picture and the rest of Docker makes sense.

cheatsheet.intro: What a container is, the programs behind `docker run`, and the commands from Lesson 1.

boards.title: What a container gets
boards.hint: an ordinary process that runs in isolation

rows.name: Its own filesystem
rows.role: It sees only the files it was started with: a small operating system's files plus the app and its libraries.

rows.name: Its own view
rows.role: Its own process numbers, network interfaces and hostname. In the lab, `sleep 600` was PID 1 inside and PID 22381 on the host.

rows.name: Limits you set
rows.role: A cap on memory and CPU. `--memory 64m` showed up inside as `memory.max` 67108864.

rows.name: One shared kernel
rows.role: `uname -r` printed the same release inside and outside. A VM boots its own kernel; a container boots nothing.

boards.note: A VM's isolation is stronger: containers that share a kernel are separated by that kernel, VMs by the hypervisor's hardware boundary. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs Linux containers inside a small Linux VM.

rows.name: docker
rows.role: The client. Sends your request to the daemon over `/var/run/docker.sock` and prints the answer.

rows.name: dockerd
rows.role: The daemon. Stores images, containers, networks and volumes, and does the work.

rows.name: containerd
rows.role: Manages images and containers on the host.

rows.name: runc
rows.role: Asks the kernel for namespaces and a cgroup and starts the process. Docker donated it to the Open Container Initiative.

rows.name: docker compose
rows.role: Compose v5.8.0, used as `docker compose` with a space. v5 is functionally identical to v2. `docker-compose` with a hyphen is the old v1.

steps.title: What the lab showed
steps.hint: IDs, process numbers and times differ on your machine

items.what: `Client 29.10.1 / Server 29.10.1` and `Docker Compose version v5.8.0`. Client and server are two programs and should be the same release.
The message lists four steps: the client contacted the daemon, the daemon pulled the image, created a container, and streamed its output back.
`docker exec sleeper ps` showed `sleep 600` as PID 1. The hostname was the container ID, and `/etc/os-release` said Alpine Linux v3.24 while the host said Ubuntu 24.04.5.
`docker top sleeper` and the host's own `ps` showed the same process as PID 22381. Nothing about it is hidden from the host.
The container's `pid`, `net`, `uts` and `mnt` namespace links had different numbers from the shell's. `memory.max` was `max` without a limit and 67108864 with `--memory 64m`.

steps.note: Safety: the `docker` group grants root-level privileges. Join it only on a machine you control, or put `sudo` in front of every `docker` command. Undo with `sudo gpasswd -d $USER docker` and a new login.

commands.cmd: sudo apt remove $(dpkg --get-selections docker.io docker-compose docker-compose-v2 docker-doc docker-buildx podman-docker containerd runc | cut -f1)
commands.note: removes conflicting packages; may find none

commands.cmd: sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

commands.note: start it with `sudo systemctl start docker`

homework.intro: Use a Linux machine with Docker Engine installed as in the lesson. IDs, process numbers and times will differ. Answers are in the separate answer key.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: In one sentence, what is a container according to Docker's guide?
exercises.a: An ordinary process on your computer that runs in isolation, with its own filesystem, its own view of processes, network and hostname, and limits you can set.

exercises.q: Which two Linux kernel features give a container its view and its limits?
exercises.a: Namespaces give it its own view (PID, mount, UTS, network and others). Control groups (cgroups) limit and monitor its use of memory and CPU.

exercises.q: Give one reason a container starts faster than a virtual machine, and one way a VM isolates more strongly.
exercises.a: A container is a process that shares the host's kernel, so there is no operating system to boot. A VM is separated by the hypervisor's hardware boundary, while containers are separated only by the shared kernel.

exercises.q: Name the four programs between typing `docker run` and your process starting, in order.
exercises.a: The `docker` client, the `dockerd` daemon, containerd, and runc, which asks the kernel for namespaces and a cgroup and starts the process.

exercises.q: Why does this series type `docker compose` and never `docker-compose`?
exercises.a: `docker compose` is the Compose plugin (v2 and later; this series uses v5.8.0). `docker-compose` with a hyphen is the old Python Compose v1, which is no longer among the supported versions.

exercises.q: Run `docker version --format 'Client {{.Client.Version}} / Server {{.Server.Version}}'`. Why are there two versions?
exercises.a: The client (`docker`) and the server (`dockerd`) are two programs that talk over a socket. In the lesson both were 29.10.1.

exercises.q: Start `sleeper` and run `docker exec sleeper ps`. What is PID 1, and why are there only two processes?
exercises.a: PID 1 is `sleep 600`, the container's command. The container has its own PID namespace, so it sees only its own processes: `sleep` and the `ps` you just ran.

exercises.q: Run `grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release` inside the container and on the host, then `uname -r` in both. What differs, and what stays the same?
exercises.a: The os-release files differ (Alpine Linux v3.24 inside, Ubuntu on the host) because the container has its own filesystem. The kernel release is the same because there is only one kernel.

exercises.q: Run `docker top sleeper`. What does the PID column show compared with `docker exec sleeper ps`?
exercises.a: The host's process number for the same process (22381 in the lesson). Inside, the same process is PID 1.

exercises.q: Run `docker run --rm --memory 64m alpine:3.24 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max`. Explain the number, and what `--rm` did.
exercises.a: 67108864 is 64 × 1024 × 1024 bytes, the 64 MiB limit, seen through the container's cgroup. `--rm` removed the container as soon as `cat` finished.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: A new user runs `docker ps` without `sudo` and before joining the `docker` group. What error do they get, and what are the two fixes?
exercises.a: `permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket`. Use `sudo`, or join the `docker` group and start a new login session (knowing that the group grants root-level privileges).

exercises.q: You run `docker run -d --name sleeper alpine:3.24 sleep 600` twice. What happens the second time?
exercises.a: It fails with `Conflict. The container name "/sleeper" is already in use`. Remove the old one with `docker rm -f sleeper`, or pick another name.

exercises.q: On the host, you compare `readlink /proc/$$/ns/net` with the container's `net` link. Will the numbers match? Why?
exercises.a: No. The container has its own network namespace, so its link shows a different identifier from your shell's.

exercises.q: After the lab, `docker ps -a` still lists a `hello-world` container with a strange name. Why is it there, and how do you remove it?
exercises.a: Each `hello-world` run leaves a stopped container behind, with a name Docker made up. Remove it by name, for example `docker rm vibrant_feistel`.
